description: We are Astral Deities, a multidisciplinary team passionate about space exploration, AI, cybersecurity, robotics, and technology that solves real-world problems.
summary:
Imagine a rover exploring the Moon’s south pole. Deep inside a shadowed crater, surrounded by steep terrain, it loses its direct line of communication with Earth. How can we restore the signal without putting another mission at risk?

This is the challenge behind AETHER Lunar Lighthouse, an interactive lunar exploration and educational platform developed by our team, ASTRAL DEITIES.

Inspired by the challenges of real lunar missions, we combined scientific data, robotics simulation, cybersecurity, and space law into one experience.

Using preliminary lunar Sun and Earth visibility data, players compare locations, evaluate environmental conditions, and control a second rover to deploy a communication relay. Every decision matters: choosing the wrong location could leave the first rover disconnected.

AETHER also offers three learning pathways for children, teenagers, and adults, making complex space science understandable through hands-on exploration, challenges, and feedback.

What makes AETHER different is that users don't just observe lunar data , they turn it into decisions. They learn how scientific evidence, engineering, and responsible decision-making come together to solve real challenges.

Our vision is to make space exploration accessible to everyone and inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers.
details:
AETHER Lunar Lighthouse — Project Details

The Problem We Wanted to Solve

Imagine a robotic rover exploring the Moon's south pole. As it travels into a deep crater, the surrounding terrain blocks its direct line of sight to Earth. The rover may still be operational, but communicating with it becomes difficult.

How could another rover help restore a potential communication path? And how can we choose a suitable location without ignoring the Moon's challenging environment?

These questions inspired AETHER Lunar Lighthouse.

What We Developed

Our team, ASTRAL DEITIES, developed an interactive lunar exploration and educational platform that brings together space science, robotics, cybersecurity, and space law.

AETHER has two main components.

1. Science Navigator

Users can explore and compare candidate lunar locations using preliminary scientific observations of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar horizon.

Our research includes 144 hourly observations for two candidate locations, CR1 and SR1, covering February 8–10, 2027. These observations help illustrate why location and timing matter when evaluating sunlight and potential Earth visibility.

2. Restore the Signal — Interactive Rover Mission

Players experience the problem through a simulation. A rover is located inside a shadowed lunar crater, and a second rover must explore the surrounding terrain, assess possible deployment positions, and place a communication relay.

The goal is to explore how terrain and line-of-sight geometry influence mission decisions.

Instead of simply watching an animation, users take part in the decision-making process. They can experiment with different approaches and learn why some choices may not work.

Technology and Development

We developed AETHER as a browser-based interactive experience, using technologies including React, JavaScript/TypeScript, Three.js, and 3D simulation tools.

Python was used in our scientific data-processing and research workflow. We also explored robotics simulation approaches and used AI-assisted development tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Replit, to support programming, research organization, and visual development.

Our approach combines scientific data analysis with a playable 3D environment, making the experience accessible through a web browser without requiring specialized hardware.

What Makes AETHER Different?

Existing lunar mapping and scientific tools provide valuable information about the Moon. Our aim was not to replace them, but to make scientific concepts easier to explore through interactive learning.

AETHER connects scientific observations to a mission scenario where users must make decisions, understand consequences, and apply what they learn.

We designed three educational pathways:

  • Junior Cadet (ages 8–11): Introducing basic robotics and lunar exploration.
  • Teen Explorer (ages 12–17): Exploring scientific reasoning, environmental challenges, and problem-solving.
  • Professional (18+): Introducing more advanced mission-planning concepts and interdisciplinary decisions.

We also considered questions beyond engineering: Who is responsible for an autonomous mission? How can communication systems be protected? What legal and ethical issues arise when operating on the Moon?

These topics help users understand that space exploration involves more than technology alone.

Scientific Accuracy and Responsible Design

Throughout development, we considered terrain, solar illumination, Earth visibility, energy limitations, communication geometry, educational accessibility, and responsible space operations.

Our scientific observations are clearly identified as preliminary and not independently verified. The rover environment is an educational simulation, not a validated real-world deployment model.

We believe communicating these limitations openly is essential to responsible scientific education.

Why It Matters

Space exploration can feel distant and complicated, especially for younger students and people without access to advanced laboratories.

We want to change that.

AETHER gives users an opportunity to explore an important space-engineering problem, experiment with possible solutions, and understand how scientific evidence supports decisions.

Our long-term vision is to develop AETHER into a broader educational platform that schools, universities, and research-oriented programs could use to introduce mission planning, robotics, and responsible exploration.

AETHER is more than a game about the Moon. It is our attempt to turn space science into an experience where anyone can explore, question, experiment, and learn.
